turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Dr. Smith. Nice to meet you too. Well, what brings me in is that I just keep getting up when I'm supposed to stay put. 

Like, during client interviews—I'm a private investigator, so I do a lot of interviewing. Most people think it's all glamorous stakeouts and hiding in bushes, but honestly, it's mostly sitting across from people in diners while they cry about their cheating spouses. I had this one client last week who brought an entire three-ring binder of printed-out text messages. Color-coded! I mean, who has the time for that? I use digital files for everything now, it's just so much easier to search and you don't have to lug a briefcase around. 

But anyway, yeah, I'm supposed to be sitting there taking notes for the case, and I just keep getting out of my chair. I do it during tutoring sessions, too. Oh, and my book club! We're reading this historical fiction about WWII spies right now, which is actually driving me crazy because the surveillance techniques they describe are completely inaccurate, but... right, the point is, people are really starting to notice that I can't just sit and listen.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states they keep getting up and getting out of their chair during situations where they are expected to stay seated, such as client interviews, tutoring sessions, and book club.

turns.doctor_question: Have you always struggled to stay seated like this since you were a child, or is this a more recent problem for you?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, definitely since I was a kid. My grade-school report cards always said I was bright but just couldn't stay in my seat or wait my turn. My mother still jokes about it, actually—she says I treated every single classroom like a crime scene I had to pace through. 

Which is funny, because real crime scenes aren't like that at all. You can't just pace through them, you have to be incredibly careful about contamination. I had this case last year—well, not a police crime scene exactly, but a suspected insurance fraud at a warehouse—and I had to wear these ridiculous little blue booties over my shoes to look around. Have you ever tried to walk quietly in those? It's impossible! They make this awful crinkling sound with every single step. Plus my feet were freezing because it was November and the building didn't have the heat on. I ended up catching a terrible cold from being in there so long, and I couldn't even take my usual cold medicine because it makes me drowsy, and you can't be drowsy on surveillance... 

Wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, school. Yeah, the getting up and pacing thing isn't new at all, it's been happening my whole life.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states they have had trouble staying in their seat since childhood and frequently get up and pace.
symptom_reasoning.S017: The patient mentions that their grade-school report cards noted they could not wait their turn.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, going off on a long, unrelated story about a warehouse and cold medicine before losing their train of thought and returning to the original topic.

turns.doctor_question: Aside from the restlessness and need to move, do you also find that you frequently struggle to maintain focus or make careless mistakes on your work tasks?
turns.patient_response:
No, not really. I mean, I'm pretty sharp when it comes to the details. You kind of have to be in my line of work, right? If you miss a license plate number or forget to log the exact time someone left a building, the whole case can fall apart. 

Actually, that reminds me of this one time I was tracking a guy who claimed he had a severe back injury, but we caught him on tape helping his buddy move a grand piano. A grand piano! Do you know how heavy those things are? My sister has one, a Steinway, and when she moved from her apartment in Chicago to this house in the suburbs, she had to hire these specialized piano movers. They had all these pulleys and straps, and it still took four guys to get it out the door. She was a nervous wreck the whole time, just pacing around and chewing her fingernails, which she hasn't done since we were in high school. She used to paint them with that awful-tasting clear polish to try and stop, but it never worked for her. 

But anyway, no, I don't really make careless mistakes. I might be up and pacing around the room while I'm reviewing the files, but I don't miss the important stuff.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient explicitly denies making careless mistakes and states they are sharp with details.
symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient answers 'No, not really' to the doctor's question about struggling to maintain focus.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient notes they are often 'up and pacing around the room' while reviewing files.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient goes on a long, unnecessary tangent about a piano, movers, and their sister's fingernails, demonstrating excessive talking.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often find yourself blurting out answers before someone has finished asking you a question, or perhaps having trouble waiting your turn in conversations or lines?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, I definitely do that. Blurting things out, I mean. It's like the answer is just right there on the tip of my tongue and I can't keep it in until they finish talking. My sister hates it when I do that, especially when we're playing trivia. We go to this pub trivia night every Thursday—well, not *every* Thursday, because sometimes I have a stakeout, but most Thursdays. 

The trivia host is this guy named Gary who wears the most ridiculous patterned shirts. Last week it was flamingos, the week before that it was pineapples... I don't know where he finds them. Probably at one of those vintage thrift stores downtown. I love those stores, actually. You can find the most amazing old cameras there. I collect vintage cameras, mostly from the 60s and 70s. I have this beautiful old Leica that I picked up for a steal because the owner didn't know what they had. I had to send it off to get refurbished, and the guy who fixed it took forever. He said he was waiting on a part from Germany, but I'm pretty sure he just forgot about it. I hate waiting for things like that. 

Oh, right, waiting in line. Yeah, I can't stand it. The grocery store, the post office... it's torture. I'm always the one tapping my foot and looking around to see if they can open another register. I just don't understand why things have to take so long!

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient mentions they are 'always the one tapping my foot' when forced to wait in line.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient provides a long, rambling response that goes off on multiple tangents about trivia, shirts, and vintage cameras, demonstrating excessive talking.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly states they blurt things out and cannot keep answers in until the other person finishes talking.
symptom_reasoning.S017: The patient describes waiting in line as 'torture' and states they cannot stand it.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often find that you lose things necessary for your work, such as your keys, phone, or important case documents, or are you generally quite organized with your belongings?
turns.patient_response:
No, I don't really lose things. I mean, my keys and phone are always right where I left them, and my case files are perfectly organized. I have this whole color-coding system for my files—red for active surveillance, blue for background checks, green for closed cases. 

I actually started using the color-coding system back when I was working at this corporate security firm. The boss there was obsessed with organization, but in the most bizarre way. He insisted that all the pens on his desk had to face the same direction, and he would literally measure the distance between his computer monitor and the edge of his desk every morning. It was exhausting just watching him. He drove a pristine vintage Corvette, cherry red, and he wouldn't let anyone park within two spaces of him in the company lot. One time, the new receptionist accidentally parked next to him because she didn't know the "rule," and he threw an absolute fit. 

She didn't last long, the receptionist. She left to go work at a bakery, which honestly sounds lovely. I love the smell of fresh bread. There's this little French bakery near my apartment that makes the most incredible croissants. They're so buttery and flaky, and they sell out by 9 AM every day, so you have to get there early. I usually grab one on my way to a stakeout, along with a large black coffee. 

But yeah, anyway, I'm pretty organized. I don't lose my stuff.

symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient talks excessively, providing a long, rambling story in response to a simple question.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangentiality, drifting from their filing system to a former boss, a receptionist, a bakery, and croissants before finally returning to the original topic.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient denies difficulty organizing, stating their files are perfectly organized using a color-coding system.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly denies losing items, stating 'No, I don't really lose things' and 'I don't lose my stuff.'
